title: The Sabbath, part 3: Romans 14, the seasons and life today

series.title: The Sabbath: God's day of rest
series.share: Three studies: the biblical Sabbath, what Jesus said about it, and Romans 14, the seasons and life today.

share: Does Romans 14 mean any day will do? Did the Father or Jesus say to keep the seasons? And how can the Sabbath work today?
opening_question: Romans 14 is often read as: worship the Father on any day, because He looks at the heart, not the calendar. Is that what it says, and how far does it go? Did the Father say to keep His feasts "in their seasons", and did Jesus? What did the apostles do, and how can a day of rest work in our society? Read every verse, also the ones Christians read in different ways, and let the text speak. This is part 3 of 3.

steps.intro: Read Romans 14 in its setting first: what is the argument about?
steps.question: Whom are the Romans to receive, and "not to doubtful disputations"? What two things do the believers disagree about, and what does Paul tell each one?
steps.apply: Do I know why I keep the day I keep, so that I am "fully persuaded" and not just following habit?

facts.text: The chapter is about "doubtful disputations": "doubtful" is dialogismos, Strong's: "debate"; "disputations" is diakrisis, "judicial estimation". It deals with matters believers were arguing over.
Two examples are given: food ("another, who is weak, eateth herbs") and days ("One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike").
The word sabbath does not stand in Romans 14, and neither does the word law. Paul does not say which days are meant.

Readers differ on which days these are. Some include the weekly sabbath. Others say Paul means fast days, feast days or days of special food, and that he would not call the fourth commandment a doubtful disputation, since he says "we establish the law".

Both sides are told the same thing: "He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord; and he that regardeth not the day, to the Lord he doth not regard it". "fully persuaded" is plerophoreo, Strong's: "completely assure".

steps.intro: How far does it go? The heart, and the commandments.
steps.question: Does the LORD look on the outward appearance or on the heart? How must true worshippers worship, what did Jesus say about love and commandments, and what does Paul say about faith and the law?
steps.apply: Do I use the thought that God looks at my heart to keep what He asks, or to excuse myself from it?

facts.text: It is true that "the LORD looketh on the heart". Jesus adds that true worshippers worship "in spirit and in truth": both together, not one instead of the other.
The heart and the commandments are joined: "If ye love me, keep my commandments"; "this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous".
Paul, who wrote Romans 14, also wrote: "Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid", and "the commandment holy, and just, and good".
Romans 14 ends: "whatsoever is not of faith is sin". Going against one's own conviction is sin, whichever way that conviction points.
It also limits how we treat others: "Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?" and "Let us not therefore judge one another any more".

steps.question: What does Paul say about being judged over "the sabbath days", what is "a shadow of things to come", and what did the Galatians "observe"?
steps.apply: Do I hold my convictions about the day with love for believers who see it differently?

facts.text: "shadow" is skia, Strong's: "shade" or "a shadow". Paul goes on: "but the body is of Christ".

Colossians 2:16 names "an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days". "holyday" is heorte, Strong's: "a festival". Some read "sabbath days" as the weekly sabbath; others as the yearly feast sabbaths and their offerings, which the list already follows.
Paul says "Let no man therefore judge you": readers differ on whether he defends those who kept these days or those who did not.

"Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years", turning again to "weak and beggarly elements". Some read this of the Jewish calendar; others of the pagan calendar the Galatians came from, since Paul says "how turn ye again".

steps.intro: Did the Father say to keep the seasons? Start at creation and Leviticus 23.
steps.question: What were the lights in the heaven made for? What does the LORD call His feasts in Leviticus 23, when were they to be proclaimed, and for how long?
steps.apply: Do I let God's calendar shape my year, or only the world's calendar?

facts.text: The lights were made "for signs, and for seasons". "seasons" is mo'ed, Strong's: "an appointment that is a fixed time or season; specifically a festival".
The same word stands in Leviticus 23: "These are the feasts of the LORD, even holy convocations, which ye shall proclaim in their seasons". God calls them "my feasts".
The weekly sabbath is the first appointed time in the list, before Passover and the rest.

The feasts are called "a statute for ever throughout your generations". The words were spoken to "the children of Israel", and three times a year their males were to "appear before the LORD" in the place He would choose.

steps.intro: Did Jesus say to keep the seasons? Look at what He did, and what He said.
steps.question: Which feasts did Jesus go up to, from the age of twelve on? What did He cry "In the last day, that great day of the feast", and what did He say at His last Passover?
steps.apply: When I remember the Lord's death, do I see how it fulfils what God set in His feasts?

facts.text: At twelve He went up to Jerusalem "after the custom of the feast". He went up to the feast of tabernacles, and was in the temple at "the feast of the dedication".
On the last day of tabernacles He cried: "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink".
"With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer". At that meal He said: "this do in remembrance of me".

The Gospels record that Jesus kept the feasts. They record no word of Jesus telling His disciples to keep the yearly feasts, and none telling them to stop. Readers draw different conclusions from His example.

steps.question: What did Paul say about Christ our passover and keeping the feast? Which feasts did he hurry to be at in Jerusalem, and what will the nations keep in Zechariah 14?
steps.apply: Whatever days I keep, do I keep them "with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth"?

facts.text: "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us": "Therefore let us keep the feast". "keep the feast" is heortazo, Strong's: "to observe a festival". Some read this as keeping Passover and Unleavened Bread in Christ; others as living a whole life of sincerity, as the verse goes on.
Paul "hasted, if it were possible for him, to be at Jerusalem the day of Pentecost".
In the King James and the Ethiopian Canon, Paul says "I must by all means keep this feast that cometh in Jerusalem". The BSB, following older Greek manuscripts, does not have these words.

Zechariah sees the nations "go up from year to year to worship the King, the LORD of hosts, and to keep the feast of tabernacles". Readers differ on whether this is literal, in a coming kingdom, or a picture of the nations' worship.

steps.intro: How Christians keep it today: three main views. Each brings its own verses; read them all and let the text speak.
steps.question: On which day did Jesus rise, and what happened "upon the first day of the week" at Troas? On what day was John "in the Spirit", and who are the saints of Revelation 14:12?
steps.apply: How does the resurrection shape my week?

facts.text: At Troas the disciples "came together to break bread" on the first day, and Paul spoke "until midnight". Counting days from sunset, that evening was Saturday night; counting from midnight, Sunday night. Readers differ on which.

"on the Lord’s day": kuriakos, Strong's: "belonging to the Lord". Many read it as Sunday; others as the sabbath, of which the Son of man is "Lord"; others as the prophetic day of the Lord. The New Testament never calls the first day the sabbath.

The seventh-day view (Seventh-day Adventists, Seventh Day Baptists, many Messianic believers): the day was blessed at creation, written in the Ten Commandments, kept by Jesus, the women and Paul, and the saints "keep the commandments of God". Many in this view keep the feasts as well.

The Lord's Day view (Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches): Christ rose on the first day and met His disciples on it, the church gathered on it "to break bread", and Revelation names "the Lord’s day". Some call Sunday the Christian Sabbath; others keep it as a day of worship without the Sabbath laws.

The rest in Christ view (many believers across churches): the sabbath was "a shadow of things to come", fulfilled in Christ, so no day is required: "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind". The council at Jerusalem did not name the sabbath among the things asked of Gentiles; others answer that it did not name stealing or lying either.

Outside history, not Scripture: Ignatius (about AD 110) and Justin Martyr (about AD 150) wrote that Christians met on the first day. In AD 321 the emperor Constantine made Sunday a day of rest by Roman law. For centuries some churches kept both days.

steps.intro: How can it work in our society? What the Bible itself gives to go on.
steps.question: What did Israel do on the sixth day, what were they to do even "in earing time and in harvest", what did Nehemiah stop at the gates, and what did Jesus say was lawful on the sabbath days?
steps.apply: What one change this week would make room for a real day of rest with God and with others?

facts.text: Prepare ahead: "on the sixth day they shall prepare that which they bring in". The Gospels call the day before "the preparation".
Busy seasons are not an exception: "in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest". Buying and selling were stopped: men "sold on the sabbath" until Nehemiah shut the gates.

Mercy is not forbidden: "it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days", and the priests in the temple worked on it "and are blameless". Many who keep the day still give care in emergencies, nursing and rescue on these grounds; others ask for the day off or change jobs.
The day is also for meeting with God's people: "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together". In the Law it is "an holy convocation".

Outside the Bible, not Scripture: in the United States, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 requires employers to reasonably accommodate an employee's day of worship unless it causes undue hardship; the Supreme Court made that test stricter in Groff v. DeJoy (2023).

steps.intro: Closing: whatever day we keep, Scripture points past the day to the rest God gives.
steps.question: What rest does Hebrews say still remains for the people of God, how do we enter it, and why did some not enter?
steps.apply: Have I entered God's rest, or am I still trying to earn what He gives?

facts.text: "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God". Here "rest" is sabbatismos, Strong's: a "sabbatism"; the BSB says "a Sabbath rest". In the rest of the chapter the word is katapausis, "reposing down".
Hebrews joins three rests: God's rest on "the seventh day", Israel's rest in the land under Joshua ("Jesus" in verse 8 is Joshua), and a rest still open: "To day if ye will hear his voice".
Those who did not enter "entered not in because of unbelief". The way in is faith: "we which have believed do enter into rest".
Readers differ: some see in Hebrews 4:9 a sabbath-keeping that remains for believers; others see the weekly sabbath fulfilled when we have "ceased from his own works" in Christ; many hold both.
